story.headline: Houthi attacks kill dozens of Yemeni troops
story.summary: Houthi missile and drone strikes on camps in Marib and Hadramout killed at least 30 government soldiers on 6 August, the deadliest escalation since the 2022 truce.
story.display_body: Houthi missile-and-drone assaults on Yemeni government camps killed at least 30 soldiers on Thursday 6 August 2026, the deadliest escalation since the 2022 truce. The Iran-backed Houthi movement struck military camps in the provinces of Marib and Hadramout, wounding around 50 more, according to Yemeni government officials; pro-government military sources put the toll higher, at 45 or above, and the Houthi spokesman claimed 'hundreds' of casualties — a figure that could not be independently verified. A de facto ceasefire between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government has largely frozen the fighting since April 2022 without any formal peace deal; officials called these coordinated strikes the most serious breach in years.
story.why: A collapse of the truce would reopen a war that had faded from view and risks drawing the Saudi-led coalition — and, indirectly, the broader Iran-US confrontation — back into open conflict.

story.headline: Netanyahu reworks Gaza disarmament deal
story.summary: Israel has rewritten the Board of Peace roadmap and Netanyahu said on 5 August that Israel will not withdraw before Hamas fully disarms, reversing the deal's core sequencing.
story.display_body: Israel has rewritten the Gaza disarmament roadmap it signed onto days earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on 5 August 2026 that Israel had 'not agreed' to withdraw before Hamas is 'completely disarmed'. Under the Board of Peace framework that US President Donald Trump announced on 30 July — the multinational body (Egypt, Qatar, Turkey and the US) overseeing the ceasefire — Hamas was to surrender its weapons in stages while Israeli forces pulled back to the agreed 'Yellow Line'; Hamas accepted that version. Le Temps reports that Israeli-imposed modifications have since decoupled Hamas's disarmament from a full Israeli withdrawal, a change Hamas says voids its participation unless Israel meets its own obligations first. The characterisation of the reworked terms is contested — Israel presents them as clarifications, mediators and Hamas as a reversal of what was agreed.
story.why: A just-announced deal is being renegotiated before implementation, leaving the ceasefire's next phase in doubt.

story.headline: Teen gunman kills five at Thai school
story.summary: A teenage student killed five people at a school near Bangkok on 7 August after fatally shooting his grandparents, before he was also killed.
story.display_body: A teenage gunman killed five people at a school on the outskirts of Bangkok on Friday 7 August 2026 after fatally shooting his grandparents at home. Police said the suspect — a student enrolled at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in Nonthaburi province — opened fire with his grandfather's handgun, firing at least 26 rounds and carrying 34 more; at least 23 people were wounded, several critically. The attacker was also killed. Authorities initially reported six dead before revising the toll to five.
story.why: Mass shootings remain rare in Thailand relative to firearm-related violence overall, and a school attack by a minor will renew scrutiny of gun access in a country with high civilian ownership.

story.headline: Meta ordered to pay $567m in New Mexico
story.summary: A New Mexico judge ruled Meta a public nuisance and ordered it to pay $567 million over harms to children, on top of $375 million in March penalties.
story.display_body: A New Mexico judge ruled Meta a 'public nuisance' and ordered it to pay $567 million over harms its apps cause to children, in a decision issued late Thursday 6 August 2026. Judge Bryan Biedscheid in Santa Fe sided with the state, directing that $420 million of the sum fund treatment services for young people and the rest go to prevention and screening over five years; the award is on top of $375 million in civil penalties a jury imposed in March. The ruling also orders Meta to block New Mexico teens' access to its apps during school hours and overnight, set their accounts to private by default, and bar minors from 'romantic or sexualised' exchanges with its AI chatbots. Meta said it disagrees and will appeal.
story.why: It is one of the largest state-level penalties yet tying a social-media platform's design to child-safety harms, and its behavioural mandates could become a template other states copy.

story.headline: Turkey sends PKK disarmament law to parliament
story.summary: Turkey submitted a framework law on 5 August setting the legal basis to disarm the PKK, a key step in the peace process, with founder Ocalan reportedly signed off.
story.display_body: Turkey submitted a long-awaited framework law to parliament on Wednesday 5 August 2026 setting the legal basis to disarm the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). The bill governs how PKK fighters lay down arms and the judicial handling of people linked to the group, and its imprisoned founder Abdullah Ocalan has reportedly signed off on the current draft. The government hopes to pass it before parliament's summer recess. Disputes remain: the PKK wants legal reforms on prosecutions and Kurdish political participation to accompany disarmament, while Ankara insists the group disarm fully first.
story.why: It is the most concrete legislative step yet in a peace process that could end one of the region's longest insurgencies, running since 1984.

story.headline: Dittli fights back with legal opinion
story.summary: Vaud state councillor Valerie Dittli released a legal opinion on 7 August finding her right to be heard was gravely violated in the Meylan report probe.
story.display_body: Vaud state councillor Valerie Dittli went on the offensive on Friday 7 August 2026, releasing a legal opinion that finds her right to be heard was 'gravely violated' during the cantonal government's handling of the Meylan report. The report, published on 24 April 2026, alleged that Dittli had secured a mandate and paid 10,000 francs of public money to the former head of a commission on agricultural land, who in return dropped a criminal complaint; a prosecutor opened a criminal investigation on the basis of it. Two constitutional-law experts commissioned by Dittli concluded the administrative-procedure guarantees were breached — deadlines too short, insufficient opportunity to respond — and Dittli, in a personal statement, called what she experienced 'extremely serious.'
story.why: The dispute over process, not just the underlying allegations, now shadows the Vaud executive and could bear on the criminal case against a sitting cantonal minister.

story.headline: US withholds F-35 audit report
story.summary: The Pentagon barred publication of a GAO report on F-35 production problems, the jet Switzerland has on order, RTS reported.
story.display_body: The US Pentagon has barred publication of a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report on F-35 production — the fighter jet Switzerland has on order — Swiss and French-language public broadcasters reported on 7 August 2026. A source told RTS the block, the first ever on a GAO report about the F-35, traces to the Pentagon; the GAO is the US federal audit office, roughly the counterpart to Switzerland's Federal Audit Office. Aviation analyst Bill Sweetman, a former Northrop Grumman manager, told RTS the report would likely show that numerous F-35 production milestones have slipped, evidence of 'very serious' programme difficulties.
story.why: Switzerland's roughly 6-billion-franc F-35 purchase has already drawn political fire over cost and delivery timing, and withheld data on schedule slippage feeds directly into that domestic debate.

story.headline: Vincenz appeal trial opens Monday
story.summary: The appeal trial of former Raiffeisen chief Pierin Vincenz opens Monday 10 August before Zurich's high court on fraud, corruption and mismanagement charges.
story.display_body: The appeal trial of former Raiffeisen chief Pierin Vincenz opens Monday 10 August 2026 before Zurich's high court, on charges of alleged fraud, corruption and criminal mismanagement. Vincenz, who ran Switzerland's third-largest banking group for years, was convicted at first instance in 2022; the appeal has been repeatedly delayed. Le Temps notes the case remains one of the highest-profile white-collar prosecutions in recent Swiss history.
story.why: The outcome will test how Swiss courts treat expense-account and self-dealing conduct at the top of a systemically important bank.

story.headline: Code beats JSON for LLM tool calls
story.summary: On BFCL v4 across 14 models, exposing tools as Python stubs matches or beats native JSON tool calls.
story.display_body: An LLM "agent" acts on the world by calling external tools. The usual method exposes each tool as a rigid JSON form the model fills in. This paper instead exposes tools as typed Python function stubs the model invokes by writing a short script — so it can chain and parallelize several calls in one turn (they call this programmatic tool calling, PTC). They run both head-to-head on BFCL v4 (the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard, a standard tool-use benchmark) across 14 models. PTC matches or beats native JSON calling in 11 of 14 models — the GPT-5.6 family gains 10.6% — matches or wins in 13 of 14 under parallel "fan-out," and stays stable under "context rot" (long, cluttered conversations) where the JSON baseline slips ~2.3%.
story.why: As agents take on more multi-step work, how you let them call tools is a real performance lever, not an implementation detail. The result — with its nod to Sutton's "bitter lesson" that general, compute-scaling methods win — says the code-native path improves as models get more capable, while the JSON path does not.

story.headline: An optimal agnostic PAC learner
story.summary: A learner matching the long-conjectured optimal sample complexity for agnostic PAC learning up to universal constants.
story.display_body: PAC learning (Probably Approximately Correct — the standard theoretical model of supervised learning) asks how many labelled examples you need to come close to the best classifier in a given family. In the harder "agnostic" setting — where you do not assume the data can be perfectly separated — a lower bound on the achievable error has been known since the 1990s, but no algorithm had been proven to match it. This paper constructs a learner whose error is provably within a single universal constant of that lower bound, for any hypothesis family of finite VC dimension (VC dimension — a standard measure of a model family's capacity).
story.why: It settles a long-standing open question in learning theory — the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning is now pinned down up to constants at every noise level. This is foundational rather than a product; the payoff is conceptual clarity about the fundamental limits of learning from data.

story.headline: Exact closed-form Muon on Stiefel manifold
story.summary: The Muon optimizer's Stiefel-manifold update has an exact closed form, yielding the Skewon algorithm.
story.display_body: Muon is a recent "matrix-aware" optimizer — it treats a weight matrix as a matrix rather than a flat list of numbers — that has drawn attention for training large models efficiently. Many problems need weights whose columns are orthonormal, i.e. points on the Stiefel manifold (the set of matrices with orthonormal columns, ubiquitous in ML and scientific computing). Existing ways to run Muon on that manifold relied on approximate or iterative inner steps. This paper shows the corresponding update has an exact closed-form solution and packages it as Skewon, a practical algorithm for orthogonality-constrained optimization, with first-order convergence guarantees in the smooth non-convex setting.
story.why: Optimizers are where a lot of quiet training efficiency lives, and this is a distinct advance in the active Muon line (the last edition covered a separate Muon-for-diffusion fix): an exact, cheap update means practitioners can enforce orthogonality without paying for an inner solver each step.

story.headline: Markov-chain routing of transformer layers
story.summary: MACRO learns task-specific skip/repeat routes through frozen LLM layers, +5% accuracy with 9x faster search.
story.display_body: Standard LLMs run their layers once, in order. "Layer routing" asks whether a different path — skipping some layers, repeating others — does better on a given task. Prior methods needed weight updates, an expensive per-example search, or ground-truth labels at inference. MACRO (Markov Chain Routing) instead learns the route as a Markov policy — a probabilistic rule that picks the next move based only on the current state — over skip, repeat and residual-add operations, leaving the model's weights untouched, then decodes high-probability routes with a top-k Viterbi search. It reports +5.0% average accuracy over unrouted baselines (largest gains on small models) and +7.2% over the best prior routing method while cutting route-search time 9.4x (14.8 to 1.6 hours).
story.why: It is a way to squeeze more out of a fixed open-weight model without retraining it — most valuable for small models running on constrained hardware, where a few points of accuracy for near-zero extra training cost is a real win.

story.headline: A model self-distills with no supervision
story.summary: U-OPSD improves LLM reasoning using only the model's own majority-vote generations, matching supervised methods.
story.display_body: Post-training methods that distill a model into itself ("on-policy self-distillation") usually still lean on an external signal — the correct answer, a reward from the environment, or guidance from a bigger model. U-OPSD (Unsupervised On-Policy Self-Distillation) removes all of it: it samples several of the model's own attempts, forms a pseudo-answer by majority vote when the model is confident enough (self-consistency), then teaches the model to reproduce that reasoning at the exact point in its longest wrong attempt where it first went off track. On math benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT25, MATH500, AMC23) it lifts Qwen3 by 8.5% and 10.7% at the 4B and 8B scales, matching or beating supervised methods (OPSD, GRPO) that use ground-truth answers.
story.why: If a model can bootstrap its own reasoning from internal consistency alone, you can improve it in domains where labelled answers are scarce or costly. The honest caveat the reader should hold onto: majority-vote self-training can also entrench mistakes the model is confidently wrong about, so gains are not guaranteed to generalize past benchmarks like these.

story.headline: Ranking-based rewards for RL reward models
story.summary: RRC derives RL rewards from relative rankings, fixing the mismatch that held generative reward models back.
story.display_body: Reinforcement learning from feedback needs a reward model to score answers. The field is shifting from discriminative reward models (which emit a single number) to generative ones (which write out a comparison or judgement) — but generative reward models are good at ranking answers against each other, not at producing the lone scalar score that RL algorithms expect, so they have underdelivered in RL. RRC (Ranking-based Reward Construction) bridges the gap by deriving the reward from relative rankings: comparing a response against its own sampled peers (self-competitive) or against a small set of reference responses (anchor-guided).
story.why: It lets the stronger, more interpretable generative reward models actually drive RL training, where until now their ranking skill did not translate into a useful learning signal. Reward modelling is the quiet bottleneck of most RL-tuned assistants, so a cleaner way to wire it up compounds.

story.headline: The illusion of visual tool-use
story.summary: A causal audit shows multimodal models' crop-and-zoom often has no causal effect on the answer.
story.display_body: The "thinking-with-images" paradigm gives multimodal models active visual operations such as crop-and-zoom, on the theory that looking closer helps. This paper builds a causal test rather than trusting accuracy numbers: it intervenes at three levels — turning tool-use on or off, corrupting everything the model sees during a run, and swapping a single observation while holding the rest of the reasoning fixed — to measure whether the returned visual evidence actually causes the answer. Its metric, Visual Evidence Gain, isolates each observation's contribution. Across six models and five perception benchmarks it finds two dominant failure modes — "Calling Without Looking" (the crop has no causal effect on the answer) and "Looking Without Planning" (the crop is informative but the model schedules it incoherently) — and shows the aggregate accuracy gain is concentrated in a small "calibrated" minority of cases.
story.why: It is a caution that the headline accuracy gains from elaborate visual-tool pipelines can be an illusion — the model may be paying extra tokens for operations that do not drive its answer. A useful diagnostic to run before deploying or trusting such systems.

story.headline: Multiplayer world models with shared state
story.summary: MASS separates a global typed world state from per-view rendering, scaling to 1024 players over 10000 steps.
story.display_body: A world model is a learned simulator that predicts how an environment will evolve. Video world models struggle with multiple players because they entangle the shared world state with each player's own view, wasting compute and drifting into view-to-view inconsistencies. MASS (Multiplayer world models with Authoritative Shared State) splits the two, exactly as a multiplayer game server does: a learned "Logic Engine" advances one global, authoritative typed state from everyone's joint actions and serves as the only recurrent memory, while a learned "Rendering Engine" draws each player's view on demand from that shared state. On a matched multiplayer Snake benchmark it beats multi-view baselines on state accuracy and cross-view consistency, and sustains 1,024 concurrent players over 10,000 steps.
story.why: It is a concrete recipe for scalable, consistent multi-agent simulation — relevant to game engines, to training environments for agents, and to any setting where many observers must share one evolving world without it fragmenting.

story.headline: Self-evolving agents poison their own skills
story.summary: Past a critical skill-pool size, added skills degrade agents irreversibly; a pre-commit gate fixes it.
story.display_body: "Self-evolving" agents get better by distilling reusable skills from their own past runs into a growing library. This paper shows the process is not monotonic: past a critical library size, newly added skills start hurting performance. The cause is structural — once a defective skill enters the decision context it becomes reference material for distilling later skills, forming cross-round contamination chains — and it is largely irreversible: deleting the original culprit afterward recovers only a small fraction of the lost performance. Their fix, Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG), screens each candidate skill with three complementary critics (structural validity, behavioral harmlessness, semantic consistency) before admission. On Terminal-Bench 2, unfiltered accumulation peaks and then decays, while VaG improves every round to 72% pass@1 with a library roughly 5x smaller, and its frozen skill set transfers to other backbones.
story.why: It is a sharp warning for the popular "just let the agent keep learning from itself" design — quality control on what enters the skill memory has to be a pre-commit gate, because by the time a bad skill's damage shows up, cleaning it out no longer undoes the harm.

story.headline: Em-dash surge marks LLMs in Congress
story.summary: Unspaced em-dash density in US congressional releases more than doubled in 2025, a population-level LLM trace.
story.display_body: LLM-assisted writing leaves faint stylistic traces; the most-discussed is the unspaced em-dash (word-word), which is normal in typeset prose but unusual in US press writing, where AP style calls for spaced dashes. In a preregistered study of 146,239 congressional press releases (480 House and Senate offices, 2021-2025), the author measured the density of unspaced em-dashes per 1,000 characters. It held at 0.10-0.12 through 2021-2024, then jumped to 0.217 in 2025 — more than double the four-year baseline — with the share of releases containing one rising from ~13% to 24.8%. The rise was net-new (plain hyphen use stayed flat), held within individual offices, and survived placebo cut-offs and falsification tests; it was symmetric across parties and chambers.
story.why: It is careful, honest evidence that LLM-assisted writing diffused broadly into official US communications by 2025 — and a model of how to measure such a claim without overclaiming. The author flags that a formal preregistered validation gate was narrowly breached, so the interpretation is offered as exploratory, and stresses the em-dash is a population-level marker, not a per-document detector: you cannot use it to catch any single release.

story.headline: US frontier-AI review goes voluntary, secret
story.summary: The White House finalized a voluntary 30-day early-access review of closed frontier models, excluding open-weight models; companies met Aug 4.
story.display_body: The White House finalised its framework for how the federal government will review advanced AI models before release, and convened major AI companies — Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta — for a staff-level meeting on Tuesday 4 August 2026 to close out the details. The framework flows from Executive Order 14409, "Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security," signed 2 June 2026, which directed agencies to stand up a voluntary scheme by 1 August 2026 under which developers give the government up to 30 days of early access to a "covered frontier model" so it can be evaluated for national-security risks such as cyber-misuse. The order and officials stress this is explicitly not licensing, pre-clearance or a permit. Two design choices stand out: a "covered frontier model" is defined as closed-source, with state-of-the-art capabilities and national-security risk — so open-weight models are excluded, and the framework states nothing in it should be read as restricting open models once they are released — and the administration is keeping the framework's contents non-public, leaving companies that were not invited, per Axios, "in the dark."
story.why: This is the US answer to the question the EU AI Act answers very differently — and the contrast matters for anyone in Switzerland building on or shipping frontier models across both markets. Where the EU's regime (whose general-purpose-AI enforcement began 2 August, covered in the last edition) is broad, binding and public, the US route is voluntary, kept secret, and aimed only at the largest closed labs. The open-weight exclusion lands in the middle of a live policy fight over whether open models are a strategic asset or a security risk. Read the national-security scoping and the secrecy as the administration's framing and choices, not as settled fact — and note that the rules companies will actually be measured against are, by design, not on the public record.

story.headline: Anthropic starts in-house chip team
story.summary: Anthropic confirmed it is hiring a silicon team to co-design custom chips with Claude models.
story.display_body: Anthropic confirmed on 5 August 2026 — in a statement to Business Insider alongside a Silicon Engineer listing on its own careers site — that it is building an in-house team to design custom chips, the first time it has publicly acknowledged the effort. The stated plan is to co-design hardware and Claude models together, with roles spanning front-end design, pre-silicon verification, physical design, analog/mixed-signal and packaging, at a $320,000-$485,000 salary band. Anthropic says its silicon is meant to sit inside a multi-vendor stack rather than replace it — a deliberate contrast with OpenAI's single purpose-built part — and, per TechCrunch, is targeting large cuts in per-token inference cost. It comes weeks after reports that Anthropic was testing AMD hardware, part of a broader loosening of Nvidia's grip on AI compute.
story.why: Frontier-lab economics are increasingly a hardware story — controlling the chip is how you control inference cost and supply. A lab hiring to design its own silicon signals it expects inference demand, and Nvidia dependence, to be a structural cost worth attacking directly. Treat the cost-reduction figure as a stated target, not a delivered result.

story.headline: MiniMax H3 open weights bar four regions
story.summary: MiniMax released 33B open-weight omni video model H3, but its license excludes the US, EU, UK and South Korea.
story.display_body: MiniMax released open weights for H3, a 33-billion-parameter dense, single-stream "omni" transformer that understands text, images, video and audio and generates video with native stereo audio at up to 2K resolution and durations up to 15 seconds. The weights — an H3-Base checkpoint in text-to-video/audio and reference-based variants — went up on Hugging Face and ModelScope. The unusual part is the licence: the MiniMax H3 Community License Agreement defines an "Applicable Territory" that excludes the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom and South Korea, meaning users in those regions are not licensed to run, modify, distribute or even use the outputs of the locally-run weights. MiniMax frames this not as excluding regions but as recognising that video-generation models face a fast-moving regulatory environment — around likeness generation, copyright and content safety — in those jurisdictions, and invites interested parties there to contact it for a bespoke, guardrail-bound licence.
story.why: This is a genuinely new twist on "open weights" — a model that is freely downloadable yet legally carved away from exactly the jurisdictions writing the strictest AI-content rules. For a Switzerland-based reader the practical note is that Switzerland is not on the excluded list, so on the face of the licence text it falls inside the Applicable Territory — but anyone actually deploying a video-generation model should read the terms and the QA notes themselves rather than rely on this summary. The territory-scoped open-weight licence is a template other labs may copy as video-generation regulation tightens.
